# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

It requires the temperance of the fire and the gradual succession of that increase, with caution, until it is fixed in its calx, lest it easily return to a metallic body, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for the perfection of its calx. Likewise, take care not to err with <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction. If, when you place its calx into reduction, it happens that it does not reduce, but you find it in its former state or reduced to glass, do not judge its reduction to be impossible. We say that if you do not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, you apply a great fire, it does not necessarily follow that it will reduce, but it is possible that it might be reduced to vitrification <note>the process of turning into a glass-like substance</note>. This is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive substance of mercury <note>original: "argenti uiui"</note> enclosed in the depth of its nature. If it endures a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and it will leave the body deprived of humidity, such that it is found more apt to be converted to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its proper humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore, it is necessary that you hasten to reduce it quickly with the most rapid force of fire. Otherwise, it will not be reduced. Practice this, therefore, and you will know.

The second mode of calcination for these two bodies, <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be projected onto their surface, quantity by quantity, very often during their fusion, and mixed by much agitation with an iron rod over the fire, until they are turned into ash by the mixture of salt. And afterwards, their calx is to be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its own considerations. But there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>lead</term> is converted into powder more easily from the initial labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its calx is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.
